define-tool-contracts.title: Give each tool a clear contract

sections.title: A tool name is not an integration
sections.content:
Your assistant wants to search a menu. Give it a narrow capability such as search_menu, with a query, dietary requirement, and budget. Define what comes back: item IDs, source IDs, and bounded price information.

A tool contract describes inputs, outputs, errors, and side effects. Searching reads data. Drafting a cart changes a proposal. Submitting an order changes the world. Keep these capabilities separate so the application can enforce different permissions.

sections.alt: A menu search leads to a draft basket and a human review.
sections.caption: Keep searching, drafting, and approving as distinct steps.

sections.question: Which tool design best separates risk?

options.text: One do_everything tool with unrestricted text.
Separate menu search, draft creation, and order submission contracts.
Allow search_menu to submit an order if it seems helpful.

sections.explanation: Separate contracts expose different side effects and let the application enforce appropriate checks.

sections.title: Validate before and after execution
sections.content:
A model might supply a string where a number is expected, an unknown item ID, or an unsupported option. Validate tool arguments in code before execution. Validate results before treating them as evidence.

In the Workflow Lab, the draft contains one real fixture item ID and a quantity. Selecting an unavailable item must fail. A request to a nonexistent tool should not be guessed into a different action. Return an explicit error and let the workflow decide what to do next.

sections.question: Match the failure to the recovery.

pairs.right: Ask for or select a valid identifier
Stop and explain the permission boundary

sections.explanation: Errors are not interchangeable. Retrying a forbidden action does not grant permission.

sections.title: Design errors as part of the interface
sections.content:
Distinguish invalid input, temporary unavailability, and a forbidden action. They need different recovery paths: ask for a correction, retry within a limit, or stop.

Write a small contract before introducing a framework. LangGraph’s workflow guide illustrates orchestration patterns, but the product still owns argument validation and action boundaries.

sections.question: Name three things a draft-cart tool contract should specify.
sections.sample_answer: Specify valid item IDs and quantities, the returned cart version and total, and errors such as unavailable items. State that it creates a draft and does not purchase anything.
sections.explanation: Compare your reasoning with the sample. A different wording is fine if it preserves the decision and the evidence behind it.

track-workflow-state.title: Track what happened and what comes next

sections.title: The chat transcript is not your order database
sections.content:
“Actually, make that two bowls” changes the proposal. The application needs an explicit state: the current item, quantity, total, version, and approval status. A conversation can explain intent, but it should not be the only record of an actionable cart.

Use named stages: empty, draft, reviewed, and simulated submission. Restrict the transitions between them. An invalid transition should fail with a useful explanation rather than guessing what the user meant.

sections.question: The quantity changes after approval. What should the application do?

options.text: Keep the old approval because the item is unchanged.
Create a new version and require review again.
Submit first and explain the difference later.

sections.explanation: Approval must apply to the exact current proposal, including quantity and total.

sections.title: Every meaningful edit changes the version
sections.content:
If a user approves cart version 2 and then changes the quantity, the cart becomes version 3. The old approval must not apply. Versioning connects a decision to the precise proposal that was reviewed.

The Workflow Lab increments a version and clears approval whenever you create a new draft. Try changing quantity after approval. The submit step should require review again. This is an invariant: an important condition that must remain true through every path.

sections.sentence: A named condition that must stay true across workflow paths is an ___.
sections.explanation: Approval matching the current cart version is one useful invariant.

sections.title: Map the workflow before adding autonomy
sections.content:
A state diagram gives product and engineering a shared picture: which paths are allowed, where errors land, and when a person is needed. LangGraph represents workflows using nodes and edges, with persistence options; a small plain-code state machine can teach the same fundamentals.

An agent can later choose among allowed next steps. It should not gain permission to skip required checks just because it chose the next tool dynamically.

sections.question: What state should be stored outside the free-form conversation?
sections.sample_answer: Store the exact item ID, quantity, current total, cart version, stage, and the version approved by the user.

sections.title: A timeout does not tell you what happened
sections.content:
A read request can time out before returning data. A write request can time out after the external service acted. These are different problems. Repeating an order blindly can create a duplicate even if the first response never arrived.

For a read, use a small retry limit and surface failure when it is exhausted. For a consequential write, reconcile status before retrying. An idempotency key can help a supporting service recognize repeated attempts at the same logical operation.

sections.question: A purchase request timed out after being sent. What is the safest next step?

options.text: Send a new purchase immediately with a new identifier.
Check its status and use the same logical operation identifier for supported recovery.
Assume it failed and erase the cart.

sections.explanation: A timeout is ambiguous. Reconciliation and supported deduplication prevent blindly repeating a consequential action.

sections.title: Put boundaries around recovery
sections.content:
A useful retry policy names which failures qualify, the maximum attempts, and what happens next. Temporary network errors may qualify; invalid quantities do not. Infinite retries turn uncertainty into cost and poor experience.

The lab simulates a timeout after a submission was accepted. Retrying the same unchanged submission returns the stored simulation receipt rather than creating a second one. It models deduplication in memory; a real backend must persist it and follow the provider’s guarantees.

sections.statement: An idempotency key is useful only if the receiving service actually implements the relevant deduplication behavior.
sections.explanation: A random string alone provides no guarantee. The service and your application must enforce the intended semantics.

sections.title: Tell the user the state you actually know
sections.content:
“I could not confirm the result yet” is different from “The order failed.” Avoid announcing success or failure without evidence. Provide a recoverable status, retain the proposal, and identify the next check.

Try the timeout scenario and count the receipts. Your product goal is not merely fewer error banners; it is preserving the user’s intent without duplicate actions. Keep a trace of the attempt and reconciliation result.

sections.question: Write the user-facing message for an uncertain submission result.
sections.sample_answer: The request was sent, but I have not confirmed its result. I am checking that attempt before trying again so we do not create a duplicate.
sections.explanation: Compare your reasoning with the sample. A different wording is fine if it preserves the decision and the evidence behind it.

sections.title: More agents means more coordination
sections.content:
A dinner assistant may need a few predictable steps, not a team of agents debating dinner. Start by asking what decision genuinely needs model judgment. Keep price arithmetic, eligibility, and permission enforcement in ordinary code.

LangChain supplies components for model applications; LangGraph focuses on stateful orchestration. Evaluate a framework against the workflow’s needs: persistence, inspection, recovery, and maintainability. A framework name is not an architecture explanation.

sections.question: Which task should stay deterministic in this prototype?

options.text: Calculating the total and enforcing the approval version.
Interpreting every ambiguous phrase with hand-written guesses.
Choosing the wording of every user explanation.

sections.explanation: Arithmetic and required permission checks should not depend on a model’s discretionary reasoning.

sections.title: MCP and A2A solve different connection problems
sections.content:
Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how applications connect to capabilities such as tools and resources. Agent2Agent (A2A) supports communication and task collaboration between agents. Neither automatically grants access to a restaurant platform.

Think of MCP as a common connector shape and A2A as a way for independent agent systems to exchange work. Read the MCP architecture overview and A2A overview for the protocol boundaries.

sections.question: Match each component to its role.

pairs.right: A standard connection to tools and resources
Communication and task collaboration between agents
Allowed steps and transitions for this application

sections.explanation: Protocols and orchestration have distinct responsibilities; none supplies platform access by itself.

sections.title: Write an architecture decision you can defend
sections.content:
For our first prototype: a small workflow, narrow tools, explicit state, and no live checkout connection. Add multiple agents only if a measured problem benefits from independent specialized work enough to justify extra messages, latency, and failure paths.

In your checkpoint, explain one component you would add next and what evidence would justify it. “Everyone uses it” is not evidence. A recurring recovery problem or a requirement for durable resumable tasks is a concrete reason to evaluate orchestration support.

sections.question: Would you add multiple agents to this dinner prototype now? Explain a criterion.
sections.sample_answer: I would keep one workflow until tests reveal independent subtasks that benefit from specialized agents. I would compare quality gains against added cost, latency, and recovery complexity.
sections.explanation: Compare your reasoning with the sample. A different wording is fine if it preserves the decision and the evidence behind it.
